title: Who Was Enoch, and What Is 1 Enoch?
bigQuestion: How did a book named after a man in Genesis 5 survive, and why did Michael Heiser think it matters for reading the Bible?

story.title: A Lost Book Comes Home
story.kicker: In 1773 a Scottish traveler reached Europe with Ethiopian manuscripts, and one held a book scholars had only known in pieces.
paragraphs: James Bruce was a tall Scottish traveler who wanted to find where the Nile River begins. In 1769 he went to Ethiopia, which Europeans then called Abyssinia. He stayed for more than two years. He learned about the country's churches, kings and old books. When he left, he packed some things he valued more than gold: handwritten books on parchment.

The books were written in Ge'ez, an old language of Ethiopia. Priests in Ethiopia still read Ge'ez in worship, the way some churches in Europe once used Latin. Among Bruce's books were three copies of one work. Its title named a man from the first pages of the Bible: Enoch.

In Europe, scholars knew that a Book of Enoch had once existed. The New Testament letter of Jude quotes a line from it. A Greek writer named George Syncellus, around 800 CE, had copied a few passages into his history of the world. But no one in Europe had the whole book. Many believed it was lost forever.

In 1773 Bruce reached Europe. He gave one copy to the royal library in Paris, and another later went to Oxford. Scholars were excited. Here was a book that people in Ethiopia had kept, copied and read in church for many centuries. It took years before anyone could translate it into English.

Today the book is called 1 Enoch. Scholars study it to learn what Jewish readers believed a few centuries before Jesus. Michael Heiser, a scholar of the Hebrew Bible, read it closely. He did not treat it as Scripture. He argued that it helps explain things the Bible's writers and first readers already knew.
story.think: Why might a book survive whole in one country but disappear almost everywhere else? What does that tell you about the people who kept it?

lessons.title: The Seventh from Adam
lessons.mainIdea: Genesis 5 gives Enoch only four verses, but they are unusual: instead of saying he died, the text says God took him.
reading: Genesis 5 is a *genealogy*, a list of family lines. It runs from Adam to Noah. Each entry follows a pattern. A man lives, has a son, lives more years, and then the text says, "and he died." The line repeats like a drumbeat through the chapter.

Enoch breaks the pattern. Genesis 5:21–24 says he had a son named Methuselah. Then he "walked with God" for three hundred years. His whole life was 365 years. The text does not say "and he died." It says he "was not," for God took him. Counting Adam as first, Enoch is the seventh name in the list.

Those few words made readers curious for centuries. What did it mean to walk with God? Where did Enoch go? Because Genesis says so little, later writers filled the gap. Many Jewish books told more stories about Enoch. The biggest of these is the book now called 1 Enoch.

words.d: a list of family members across generations, like a family tree written as a list
Enoch's son in Genesis 5; the Bible says he lived 969 years, the longest of anyone listed

look.title: Genesis 5:24
look.text: And Enoch walked with God: and he was not; for God took him.
look.prompt: Compare this verse with the other entries in Genesis 5, which end "and he died." What is different, and why would readers notice it?

check.q: What kind of chapter is Genesis 5?
choices: A genealogy, a list of family lines from Adam to Noah
A song about the creation of the world
A set of laws for priests
check.why: Genesis 5 lists generations from Adam to Noah, which is what a genealogy is.

check.q: How is Enoch's entry in Genesis 5 different from the others?
choices: It is the longest entry in the chapter
It does not end with "and he died"; it says God took him
It says he built a city
check.why: Genesis 5:24 says Enoch "was not, for God took him," breaking the pattern of "and he died."

check.q: Counting Adam as first, where does Enoch come in the Genesis 5 list?
check.why: Enoch is seventh from Adam. The letter of Jude also calls him "the seventh from Adam."

lessons.title: What Does "God Took Him" Mean?
lessons.mainIdea: Readers have explained Genesis 5:24 in different ways, and later books like Hebrews and Jubilees added their own understanding.
reading: The phrase "God took him" is short, and readers have understood it in more than one way. Many Jewish and Christian readers believed Enoch went to God without dying. The New Testament book of Hebrews reads it this way. Hebrews 11:5 says Enoch was "translated," or carried away, so that he would not see death.

Other readers thought the phrase could be a gentle way to describe a death. They pointed out that Enoch's life of 365 years is short compared with the others in Genesis 5. Some ancient Jewish interpreters leaned toward this view. The text itself does not explain what happened, so each reading fills a silence.

Later Jewish books made Enoch a great teacher and writer. The book of *Jubilees*, from around 150 BCE, says Enoch was the first person to learn writing. It says he wrote down signs of the heavens and testified against the Watchers. In these books Enoch becomes a scribe who sees heavenly things and reports them.

words.d: a Jewish book from about 150 BCE that retells Genesis and part of Exodus with extra details
in the King James Version of Hebrews 11:5, carried from one place to another; here, taken to God

look.title: Hebrews on Enoch
look.text: By faith Enoch was translated that he should not see death; and was not found, because God had translated him: and before his translation he had this testimony, that he pleased God.
look.prompt: How does Hebrews 11:5 explain the short phrase in Genesis 5:24? What does it add that Genesis does not say?

check.q: How does Hebrews 11:5 read the words "God took him"?
choices: Enoch built a tower to heaven
Enoch was punished for a wrong choice
Enoch left to live in another country
Enoch was carried away so that he would not see death
check.why: Hebrews 11:5 says Enoch was "translated that he should not see death."

check.q: Which book, from around 150 BCE, says Enoch was the first person to learn writing?
check.why: Jubilees, a Jewish retelling of Genesis, presents Enoch as the first to learn writing.

check.q: Why do readers disagree about what happened to Enoch?
choices: Genesis says he became an angel
Genesis does not explain what "God took him" means
Genesis tells the story twice in different ways
check.why: Genesis 5:24 is very short, so different readings try to fill in what the text leaves unsaid.

lessons.title: Three Books Named Enoch
lessons.mainIdea: Three different ancient books carry Enoch's name; this unit is about 1 Enoch, the oldest of them.
reading: Because Genesis says so little about Enoch, writers in later centuries wrote books in his name. Scholars number them to keep them apart. They are 1 Enoch, 2 Enoch and 3 Enoch. The numbers do not mean they are volumes of one series. They are three separate books from different times and places.

*1 Enoch* is the oldest. Its earliest parts come from about 300 BCE. It survives whole in Ge'ez, the old language of Ethiopia, so it is sometimes called Ethiopic Enoch. 2 Enoch survives in Old Church Slavonic, a language of early Slavic churches, and is called Slavonic Enoch. 3 Enoch is written in Hebrew and comes from much later Jewish writers.

When the New Testament letter of Jude quotes Enoch, the words match 1 Enoch. When Michael Heiser wrote about Enoch and the Watchers, he meant 1 Enoch. So in this unit, "the Book of Enoch" always means 1 Enoch. Knowing which book is meant is the first step in checking any claim about it.

words.d: the oldest book written in Enoch's name, made of five parts from about 300 BCE to the first century CE
an ancient language of Ethiopia, still used in worship in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches

look.title: Which Enoch?
look.text: A website says, "The Book of Enoch was written in Slavonic." Another says, "The Book of Enoch was found in the Dead Sea Scrolls." A third says, "The Book of Enoch was written in Hebrew in the Middle Ages." Each statement is partly about a different book.
look.prompt: Match each statement to 1 Enoch, 2 Enoch or 3 Enoch. What question would you ask before trusting a claim about "the Book of Enoch"?

check.q: Which book named after Enoch is the oldest?
choices: All three were written in the same year
check.why: 1 Enoch is the oldest; its earliest parts date from about 300 BCE.

check.q: In which language does 1 Enoch survive complete?
choices: Ge'ez, the old language of Ethiopia
check.why: 1 Enoch survives whole in Ge'ez, which is why it is also called Ethiopic Enoch.

check.q: When the letter of Jude quotes Enoch, which book do the words match?
check.why: Jude 14–15 matches a line from 1 Enoch 1:9.

lessons.title: Five Books Inside One
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch is really five shorter books joined together, and scholars name each part.
reading: Open 1 Enoch and you will find 108 chapters. But scholars see that it is not one book written at one time. It is a collection of five parts. Each part has its own style and its own main subject. Later copyists put them together under Enoch's name.

The first part is the *Book of the Watchers*, chapters 1–36. It tells of heavenly beings who came down to earth. Next come the *Parables*, chapters 37–71, visions of a heavenly judge. The Astronomical Book, chapters 72–82, is about the sun, moon and a calendar. The Dream Visions, chapters 83–90, retell history as a dream. The Epistle of Enoch, chapters 91–108, is Enoch's advice to his children.

Knowing the five parts helps you read carefully. A claim about 1 Enoch might be true of one part but not another. For example, the story of the Watchers comes from the first part. The Parables are the part missing from the Dead Sea Scrolls. You will learn more about that in a later lesson.

words.d: 1 Enoch 1–36, the first and one of the oldest parts, about heavenly beings who came down to earth
1 Enoch 37–71, visions about a heavenly judge; also called the Similitudes
in 1 Enoch and Daniel 4, a name for heavenly beings; in 1 Enoch, the ones who came down to earth

look.title: Chapters in Each Part of 1 Enoch

look.prompt: Which two parts are the longest? Together, what share of the whole book do they fill?

check.q: How many parts do scholars find in 1 Enoch?
check.why: Scholars divide 1 Enoch into five parts, from the Book of the Watchers to the Epistle of Enoch.

check.q: Which part of 1 Enoch tells about the Watchers coming down to earth?
choices: The Book of the Watchers, chapters 1–36
check.why: The Book of the Watchers, 1 Enoch 1–36, holds the story of the Watchers.

check.q: What is the Astronomical Book mainly about?
choices: The sun, the moon and a calendar
check.why: The Astronomical Book, 1 Enoch 72–82, describes the movements of the sun and moon and a calendar.

lessons.title: Written Over Three Centuries
lessons.mainIdea: The five parts of 1 Enoch were written at different times, from about 300 BCE to the first century CE.
reading: Scholars date ancient books by clues. They look at the oldest copies, at the events a book seems to know about, and at its language. For 1 Enoch these clues point to a long period of writing. The parts were written over roughly three hundred years.

The Book of the Watchers and the Astronomical Book are the oldest. Many scholars date them to around 300–200 BCE. The Dream Visions seem to know about the Maccabean revolt, a Jewish uprising in the 160s BCE. So they are dated to about that time. The Epistle of Enoch is probably from the 100s BCE.

The Parables are the youngest part. Many scholars date them to the late first century BCE or the first century CE. That is close to the time of Jesus. Scholars still discuss the exact dates, so books give ranges. When you read a date for 1 Enoch, ask which part it describes.

words.d: a Jewish uprising in Judea in the 160s BCE against the Greek-speaking Seleucid king
a span of years in which scholars think a text was written, used when an exact year is unknown

look.title: Clues for Dating a Book
look.text: Three clues about a part of 1 Enoch: (1) Pieces of it were found in caves where scrolls were hidden before 70 CE. (2) Its dream story seems to describe a war in the 160s BCE. (3) Its language matches Aramaic used in Judea in that period.
look.prompt: What can each clue tell you about when the text was written? Which clue gives a latest possible date, and which gives an earliest?

check.q: Which parts of 1 Enoch are the oldest?
choices: The Book of the Watchers and the Astronomical Book
The Dream Visions and the Parables
All parts were written in the same year
check.why: Many scholars date the Book of the Watchers and the Astronomical Book to about 300–200 BCE.

check.q: Why are the Dream Visions dated to about the 160s BCE?
choices: They name the year they were written
They seem to know about the Maccabean revolt
They were found in a church in Paris
check.why: The Dream Visions appear to describe the Maccabean revolt of the 160s BCE.

check.q: Which part of 1 Enoch is probably the youngest?
check.why: Many scholars date the Parables to the late first century BCE or the first century CE.

lessons.title: Writing in an Ancient Hero's Name
lessons.mainIdea: Scholars think 1 Enoch was written by later Jewish writers who used Enoch's name, a common practice in their time.
reading: 1 Enoch is written as if Enoch himself is speaking. Enoch lived before the flood in the Genesis story. But the book's oldest parts come from about 300 BCE. So most scholars think later Jewish writers composed it and put it in Enoch's voice.

Writing in the name of a famous figure from the past was common in the ancient world. Scholars call such books *pseudepigrapha*, which means "falsely titled" in Greek. The word is a technical label, not an insult. Writers used a great name to show that their message fit an honored tradition. Other examples include books written in the names of Moses, Baruch and Ezra.

Why choose Enoch? Genesis says he walked with God and was taken. That made him a perfect person to tell heavenly secrets. A man who had been close to God could describe heaven, angels and the end of days. Readers today can study the book while knowing who probably wrote it and when.

words.d: ancient writings credited to a famous figure from the past who did not write them; a scholars' label, not an insult
beliefs, stories and practices handed down over time within a community

look.title: Why Borrow a Great Name?
look.text: A writer around 250 BCE wants to warn people that heavenly beings who break God's order will be judged. He writes the message as Enoch, a man Genesis says walked with God and was taken away before the flood.
look.prompt: What would the writer gain by using Enoch's voice instead of his own? What might a careful reader today want to know about the real author?

check.q: What does the scholars' term pseudepigrapha describe?
choices: Books translated from Greek into Latin
Books credited to a famous past figure who did not write them
check.why: Pseudepigrapha are writings put in the name of an honored figure from the past.

check.q: Why do most scholars think Enoch did not write 1 Enoch himself?
choices: Its oldest parts come from about 300 BCE, long after the Genesis setting
check.why: The oldest parts date to about 300 BCE, so scholars think later writers used Enoch's name.

check.q: Why was Enoch a good figure for a book about heavenly secrets?
choices: Genesis says he walked with God and was taken
He was a king of Babylon
check.why: Genesis 5:24 describes Enoch as close to God, which made him fitting for visions of heaven.

lessons.title: Kept in Ethiopia
lessons.mainIdea: The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church kept 1 Enoch in its Bible, which is why the whole book survives.
reading: Ethiopia has one of the oldest Christian traditions in the world. Its church became Christian in the 300s CE. Early on, Christians there translated many books into Ge'ez. One of those books was Enoch. Scholars think it was translated from a Greek version, perhaps around 400–600 CE, though estimates vary.

The *Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church* counts 1 Enoch as part of its Bible. So does the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church. Scribes there copied it by hand, generation after generation. Because they kept copying it, the whole book survived there when it was lost elsewhere.

A book that belongs in a church's Bible is part of its *canon*. Different churches have different canons. Ethiopian Christians read 1 Enoch in their worship. For them it is not a lost book or a strange book. It is part of the Scripture they have always had.

words.d: the ancient Christian church of Ethiopia, whose Bible includes 1 Enoch and Jubilees
the list of books a religious community accepts as its Scripture
a person trained to copy texts by hand

look.title: One Book, Two Views
look.text: A student in Addis Ababa hears 1 Enoch read in church as Scripture. A student in Chicago finds 1 Enoch on a library shelf labeled "ancient Jewish writings." Both students are holding the same book.
look.prompt: How can the same book be Scripture for one community and a historical source for another? How would you describe the book fairly to both students?

check.q: Which church includes 1 Enoch in its Bible?
check.why: 1 Enoch is canonical in the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church and the Eritrean Orthodox Church.

check.q: What does canon mean?
choices: The list of books a community accepts as its Scripture
check.why: A canon is the set of books a religious community counts as Scripture.

check.q: Why did the whole of 1 Enoch survive in Ethiopia?
choices: It was carved on stone walls
It was buried in a cave
Scribes there kept copying it as part of their Bible
check.why: Ethiopian scribes copied 1 Enoch generation after generation because it was in their canon.

lessons.title: From Ethiopia to Europe
lessons.mainIdea: James Bruce brought 1 Enoch to Europe in 1773, and English translations followed, including R. H. Charles's.
reading: Before 1773, European scholars knew only bits of 1 Enoch. They had the quotation in Jude. They had Greek passages copied by George Syncellus, a writer from around 800 CE. The rest seemed lost. Then James Bruce, a Scottish traveler, returned from Ethiopia with copies in Ge'ez.

Few people in Europe could read Ge'ez, so translation took time. In 1821 Richard Laurence, a scholar at Oxford, published the first English translation. Later the Irish scholar *R. H. Charles* studied many more manuscripts and made a careful new translation. He published it in 1912, and a popular edition followed in 1917.

Charles's 1917 translation is now in the public domain. That means anyone may copy and quote it freely. This course uses it when it cites chapter and verse in 1 Enoch. Modern translations exist too, based on even more manuscripts, including pieces found later in the Dead Sea Scrolls.

words.d: an Irish scholar whose English translation of 1 Enoch (1912; popular edition 1917) is still widely used
no longer under copyright, so anyone may copy and quote it
a text copied by hand, before printing

check.why: James Bruce, a Scottish traveler, returned from Ethiopia with Ge'ez copies of 1 Enoch.

check.q: What did George Syncellus contribute before 1773?
choices: He translated the whole book into English
He copied some Greek passages of Enoch into his history
He found the Dead Sea Scrolls

check.why: Around 800 CE Syncellus copied Greek passages of Enoch, one of the few pieces Europe had.

check.q: Why can this course quote R. H. Charles's 1917 translation?

lessons.title: Pieces in the Caves
lessons.mainIdea: Aramaic pieces of 1 Enoch found among the Dead Sea Scrolls show the book was read in Judea before Jesus's time.
reading: Between 1947 and 1956, people found ancient scrolls in caves near Qumran, by the Dead Sea. These are the *Dead Sea Scrolls*. Most were torn into small pieces. In Cave 4, found in 1952, scholars identified pieces of about eleven copies of Enoch writings, written in *Aramaic*.

Aramaic was a common language of Judea in that period. Scholars think Aramaic was probably the original language of much of 1 Enoch. The scholar J. T. Milik published these Aramaic pieces in 1976. Some of the copies are among the oldest scrolls found, from around 200 BCE.

One part was missing. No piece of the Parables, chapters 37–71, has been found at Qumran. Scholars treat this as one clue that the Parables are later than the other parts. The finds showed that Jewish readers knew the Book of the Watchers well before the New Testament was written.

words.d: about 900 ancient Jewish manuscripts found in caves near Qumran, 1947–1956
a language related to Hebrew, widely spoken in Judea around the time of Jesus
a site near the Dead Sea where caves held many of the Dead Sea Scrolls

choices: Jewish readers knew parts of it before the New Testament was written

check.why: Copies from around 200 BCE show that Jewish readers in Judea knew the book long before the New Testament.

lessons.title: In Some Bibles, Not Others
lessons.mainIdea: 1 Enoch is Scripture only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox churches, though early Christians discussed it and Jude quotes it.
reading: 1 Enoch is not in the Jewish canon, the Hebrew Bible. It is not in the Roman Catholic, Eastern Orthodox or Protestant Bibles either. It is canonical only in the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo churches. Other communities read it as an important ancient writing, not as Scripture.

Still, New Testament writers knew it. The letter of *Jude*, verses 14–15, quotes 1 Enoch 1:9. Jude calls Enoch "the seventh from Adam" and repeats his warning that the Lord comes with many thousands of holy ones. Readers disagree on what Jude meant by quoting it. Some say he honored the book; others say he only used a line his readers knew.

Early Christian writers also disagreed. Tertullian, around 200 CE, defended the book. Augustine, in the 400s, did not accept it as Scripture. Over time most churches left it out. The debate shows that deciding a canon was a long conversation, not a single moment.

words.d: a short New Testament letter; verses 14–15 quote 1 Enoch 1:9
counted as part of a community's Scripture

look.cite: Jude 14, King James Version (1611); compare 1 Enoch 1:9 in R. H. Charles (1917)
look.prompt: Jude quotes a book that is not in most Bibles. What are two different ways a reader might explain why Jude did this?

check.q: Which New Testament book quotes 1 Enoch 1:9?
check.why: Jude 14–15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9 and calls Enoch "the seventh from Adam."

check.q: In which Bibles is 1 Enoch canonical?
choices: The Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox Bibles

check.q: How did Tertullian and Augustine differ about 1 Enoch?
choices: Tertullian defended it; Augustine did not accept it as Scripture
check.why: Tertullian, around 200 CE, argued for it, while Augustine in the 400s did not accept it.

lessons.title: Heiser: A Window, Not Scripture
lessons.mainIdea: Heiser did not treat 1 Enoch as Scripture, but he argued it shows what New Testament writers and readers already knew.
reading: Michael Heiser studied the Hebrew Bible and ancient Semitic languages. He wrote about 1 Enoch in Reversing Hermon (2017) and in A Companion to the Book of Enoch (2020). In those books he said plainly that he did not consider 1 Enoch Scripture. He read it as a *Second Temple* Jewish text, written between about 500 BCE and 70 CE.

Heiser argued that the book is a window. It shows how many Jews read Genesis 6 around the time of Jesus. He pointed to New Testament passages that seem to assume the Watchers story. Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels who sinned and are kept in chains for judgment. 2 Peter uses the Greek word *Tartarus* for their prison, a word also found in the Greek of 1 Enoch.

Other scholars agree that 1 Enoch shaped some New Testament language. They differ on how much. Some think the links are few and loose. Heiser thought the links were many and important. You can test the idea yourself by reading the passages side by side.

words.d: the time from about 500 BCE to 70 CE, when the second Temple stood in Jerusalem
a Greek word for a deep prison below the world; 2 Peter 2:4 uses a verb from it for where sinning angels are held

look.title: 2 Peter on Angels Who Sinned

look.prompt: Heiser said passages like this assume readers know the Watchers story. What details here match what you have learned about 1 Enoch?

check.why: Many scholars see some links, but some think they are fewer and less important than Heiser argued.
